description: What inflation is, how the CPI measures it, demand-pull vs cost-push, and who wins and loses from rising prices.
content_html:
What Is Inflation?

Inflation is a sustained rise in the general price level. Notice two key words: “sustained” and “general.” A single supermarket putting up its price of bread by 10p is not inflation. Inflation occurs when prices across the whole economy — food, fuel, rent, clothing, leisure — rise persistently over months and years.

The rate of inflation tells you how fast prices are rising. If the price level rose by 3% last year, the inflation rate was 3%. A student spending £50 a week on essentials would find that same basket costing £51.50 a year later at 3% inflation — modest, but over several years the cumulative effect becomes significant.

Two related terms are worth knowing. Deflation is when the general price level falls. This sounds like good news for shoppers, but it can be damaging: if consumers expect prices to fall further, they delay spending, demand drops, firms cut output and jobs, and the economy can spiral downwards. Disinflation is different: prices are still rising, but the rate of increase is slowing. If inflation falls from 5% to 2%, that is disinflation, not deflation.

Key Fact

The Bank of England has a target of keeping inflation at 2% as measured by the Consumer Prices Index (CPI). This target is set by the government. When CPI inflation is more than 1 percentage point above or below the 2% target (i.e. above 3% or below 1%), the Bank of England Governor must write a formal open letter of explanation to the Chancellor.

Measuring Inflation: The Consumer Prices Index

The Consumer Prices Index (CPI) is the main way inflation is measured in the UK. The Office for National Statistics (ONS) surveys approximately 750 goods and services — a “basket” representing typical household spending. Every month, trained collectors check the prices of these items in shops, supermarkets and online.

The basket is weighted to reflect how households actually spend their money. Rent and food take larger weights than, say, foreign holidays, because most families spend more on those items. The percentage change in the total index from one year to the next gives the CPI inflation rate.

You can also use CPI figures to calculate real changes. If a worker’s wage rises by 4% but CPI inflation is 5%, their real wage has fallen — they can buy less with their higher nominal pay. The calculation is straightforward: real change ≈ nominal change − inflation rate. This matters because exam questions regularly ask you to interpret CPI data.

These three terms trip students up constantly. Inflation: prices are rising (e.g. CPI = +3%). Disinflation: prices are still rising, but more slowly (e.g. CPI falls from 5% to 2%). Deflation: prices are actually falling (e.g. CPI = −1%). A quick test: if the CPI is positive, prices are going up — you have inflation. If the CPI is negative, prices are falling — that is deflation. Disinflation is just the rate of inflation decreasing; you still have inflation, just less of it.

Deflation is often treated as worse than mild inflation. When prices fall, consumers postpone big purchases (“I’ll wait until it’s cheaper”), reducing demand. Firms then cut output and reduce wages or jobs. This can create a deflationary spiral that is very hard to escape. Japan experienced persistent deflation for much of the 1990s and early 2000s, with damaging effects on growth.

Causes of Inflation

Economists identify two main routes through which inflation can develop: demand-pull and cost-push. Understanding the difference matters, because the appropriate policy response can differ.

Demand-pull inflation occurs when total demand in the economy rises faster than the economy’s productive capacity. Think of it as “too much money chasing too few goods.” Imagine the government cuts taxes sharply, households have more take-home pay, consumer spending surges, and retailers find their shelves emptying fast. Faced with excess demand, sellers raise prices. The chain is: demand rises → output cannot keep up → prices are bid upwards. Demand-pull inflation is typically associated with a booming economy where unemployment is low and confidence is high.

Cost-push inflation comes from the supply side. If the costs of production rise — raw materials become more expensive, wages go up faster than productivity, or energy prices spike — firms pass those higher costs on through higher prices. For example, if world oil prices rise sharply, haulage and manufacturing costs climb, and price rises ripple across the whole economy. Cost-push inflation is particularly uncomfortable because it is accompanied by slower growth: the economy gets more expensive at the same time as output is squeezed.

Key Fact

Demand-pull: demand rises faster than supply → excess demand → prices rise. Cost-push: production costs rise (wages, raw materials, energy) → firms raise prices to protect profit margins → general price level rises. Both produce inflation, but via opposite routes — one from excess demand, one from squeezed supply.

A quick rule: ask “Is this caused by more spending (demand), or by higher production costs (supply)?” Rising consumer confidence and spending → demand-pull. Rising global commodity prices, higher minimum wage, or falling pound making imports dearer → cost-push. In reality the two can combine: a booming economy (demand-pull) bids up wages (which then also acts as cost-push), but the distinction matters for your written answers.

Consequences of Inflation

Inflation does not affect everyone equally. Who wins and who loses depends on their economic position.

Consumers: Real purchasing power falls if wages do not keep up with prices. Those on fixed incomes — for example, retired people relying on a pension that does not rise with inflation — are particularly hard hit. The cost of everyday items (food, fuel, energy bills) absorbs a rising share of take-home pay.

Savers: Inflation erodes the real value of savings. If a saver earns 1% interest but inflation is 4%, the real return is −3%. Their £1,000 deposit can buy less in a year’s time than it can today.

Borrowers: Inflation can benefit borrowers. The real value of a fixed debt falls when prices rise: a £10,000 loan feels lighter to repay in real terms when average prices have gone up. This is one reason governments can benefit from moderate inflation if they carry large national debts.

Firms: Unpredictable inflation makes planning difficult. Firms cannot be sure what their costs will be next year, which discourages long-term investment. If UK inflation is higher than in competitor countries, UK exports become less price-competitive abroad, harming the balance of payments. However, firms with market power may be able to raise prices faster than their costs rise, temporarily boosting profit margins.

Workers: If pay rises lag behind inflation, real wages fall and living standards decline. Workers may then demand higher nominal wages, which can feed back into cost-push inflation — this self-reinforcing cycle is sometimes called a “wage-price spiral.”

Why Price Stability Matters

Price stability — keeping inflation close to 2% — is a central government objective because it creates a predictable economic environment. When businesses can forecast their costs reliably, they invest more. When consumers know prices will not leap unpredictably, confidence is higher. Low and stable inflation also protects those on fixed incomes and keeps the real value of savings intact.

Governments can use monetary policy (changing interest rates through the Bank of England) to manage inflation. If inflation is too high, the Bank of England raises the bank rate → borrowing costs more → consumers spend less and firms invest less → demand in the economy falls → upward pressure on prices eases. Fiscal policy can also play a role: a government can raise taxes or cut spending to reduce aggregate demand and cool demand-pull inflation.
exam_tip_html: The command word “Explain” requires a chain of reasoning, not just a label. Don’t write “inflation harms savers.” Write: “Inflation reduces the real value of savings because the interest earned may be less than the rate of price rises, meaning the purchasing power of the money falls.” For “Analyse” questions, always trace cause and effect all the way through to the final outcome (e.g. rising oil prices → higher production costs → firms raise prices → CPI rises). For “Evaluate” questions, you must consider both sides and reach a supported judgement — for example, consider who is harmed by high inflation but also whether any group benefits, and whether the significance depends on the size of the inflation rate or the time period involved.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Inflation is a sustained rise in the general price level, measured by the CPI. The Bank of England targets 2% inflation. Disinflation is a slowdown in inflation; deflation is when prices actually fall.
  • Demand-pull inflation is caused by excessive demand; cost-push inflation is caused by rising production costs such as higher wages or dearer raw materials.
  • Inflation redistributes from savers and those on fixed incomes towards borrowers. Price stability benefits everyone by making planning, investment and everyday budgeting more predictable.

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following best describes the Consumer Prices Index (CPI)?
A) A measure of the total output of the UK economy
B) A measure of average changes in prices paid by consumers for a basket of goods and services
C) The interest rate set by the Bank of England
D) The total amount of government borrowing in one year
practice_questions.marks: B) A measure of average changes in prices paid by consumers for a basket of goods and services [1 mark]

practice_questions.text:
A household's weekly shopping basket cost £80 last year. The CPI inflation rate over the past year was 5%. Calculate the new cost of the basket.
Show your working.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for the correct method: £80 × 1.05 (or £80 + (£80 × 5 ÷ 100)); 1 mark for the correct answer of £84.

practice_questions.text: Explain why deflation can be harmful to an economy.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for stating that deflation means prices are falling; 1 mark for explaining that consumers may delay spending because they expect prices to fall further; 1 mark for developing the chain — lower spending reduces firms' revenue, leading to lower output and job cuts, which can create a downward spiral in the economy.

practice_questions.text: A large rise in global oil prices pushes up transport and energy costs for UK firms. Using your knowledge of cost-push inflation, explain how this is likely to affect UK consumers.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying this as cost-push inflation (rising production costs); 1 mark for explaining that higher costs lead firms to raise prices to protect profit margins; 1 mark for linking to the general price level rising (inflation increasing); 1 mark for developing the impact on consumers — real purchasing power falls, especially for those on fixed incomes who cannot compensate through higher wages.

practice_questions.text: Analyse how a sustained period of high inflation might affect savers, borrowers and firms in the UK economy.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (5–6 marks): A connected chain of cause and effect covering at least two of the three groups. Savers: the real value of savings falls if the interest rate is below the inflation rate, reducing purchasing power. Borrowers: benefit because the real value of a fixed debt falls over time. Firms: face uncertainty in planning and investment, rising input costs may squeeze margins, and if UK inflation is higher than abroad, exports become less competitive. Response integrates the groups or identifies trade-offs between them.

Secure (3–4 marks): Correct analysis of at least two groups with some development, but chains of reasoning may not be fully completed or linked together.

Developing (2 marks): Identifies effects on one or two groups without developing the reasoning.

Emerging (1 mark): A simple point about inflation with limited application to the groups.

practice_questions.text:
'The most damaging consequence of high inflation is its impact on people with savings.' To what extent do you agree with this view?
In your answer, consider the effects of inflation on different groups in the economy and reach a supported judgement.
practice_questions.marks:
Arguments in support:
- Savers see the real value of their money eroded: if inflation is 4% but bank interest is 1%, the real return is -3%, meaning purchasing power falls every year.
- Retired people relying on fixed pension income are particularly vulnerable — they cannot increase earnings as working households might.
- Over time, erosion of savings can reduce consumer confidence and spending.

Arguments against:
- Borrowers actually benefit from inflation as the real value of debt falls — households with mortgages and businesses with loans gain.
- Workers who successfully negotiate wage rises above the inflation rate see their real incomes rise, suffering little harm.
- Firms with market power may raise prices faster than costs, temporarily boosting profits.
- The damage to the economy's competitiveness (exports become pricier) and to investment planning (uncertainty) may be as significant as the impact on savers.

Judgement: The significance of the impact on savers depends on the level of interest rates relative to inflation, the size of savings held, and the time period. During periods of high inflation combined with low interest rates (as seen following global financial shocks), the real loss to savers can be severe. However, if the inflation is demand-pull and is accompanied by rising employment and wages, many households may be insulated. A more complete judgement might conclude that the most harmful consequence is the unpredictability inflation creates across the whole economy, as this discourages investment — which harms future growth and living standards for everyone.

Mastering (8–9 marks): Developed arguments on both sides, several affected groups analysed, a specific supported judgement that uses 'it depends on' reasoning (level of interest rates, type of inflation, time period).

Secure (5–7 marks): Clear arguments for and against with some development, a judgement present but may lack qualification.

Developing (3–4 marks): Some relevant points on both sides; limited development; judgement may be asserted rather than supported.

Emerging (1–2 marks): Simple points, one-sided or list-based; little analysis.

knowledge_checks.q: What is the term for a slowdown in the rate of inflation, where prices are still rising but more slowly?
Which type of inflation is caused by rising production costs such as higher energy or raw material prices?
The Bank of England aims to keep inflation at _____ percent as measured by the CPI.
Demand-pull inflation occurs when total demand rises faster than the economy's _____ capacity.
Match each term to its correct meaning:
right: A sustained rise in the general price level
A fall in the general price level
An index tracking average consumer prices using a representative basket

flashcard_questions.a: A sustained rise in the general price level of goods and services across the economy.

flashcard_questions.q: What is the Bank of England's CPI inflation target?
What does CPI stand for, and who calculates it in the UK?
flashcard_questions.a: Consumer Prices Index; calculated by the Office for National Statistics (ONS).

flashcard_questions.q: Deflation is when the general price level is _____.
Disinflation means prices are still _____, but the rate is _____ than before.

flashcard_questions.a: Total demand rising faster than the economy can increase output.
Rising production costs — such as higher wages, energy or raw material prices.

flashcard_questions.q: How does high inflation affect someone with savings earning 1% interest when inflation is 4%?
flashcard_questions.a: Their real return is -3%; the purchasing power of their savings falls.

flashcard_questions.q: Why can borrowers benefit from inflation?
flashcard_questions.a: The real value of a fixed debt falls as prices rise, so the loan is cheaper to repay in real terms.
Workers demand higher wages to match rising prices, which raises firms' costs, pushing prices higher still.

flashcard_questions.q: Cloze: If a worker's wage rises 3% but inflation is 5%, their real wage has _____ by roughly ____%.
Why does high inflation make long-term business investment more difficult?
flashcard_questions.a: Unpredictable costs make it hard to forecast profits, so firms are more reluctant to commit to investment.

flashcard_questions.q: How can the Bank of England use interest rates to reduce demand-pull inflation?
flashcard_questions.a: Raise interest rates → borrowing costs more → spending and investment fall → demand eases → price rises slow.

glossary_terms.definition: A sustained rise in the general price level of goods and services in an economy over time.
The percentage change in the price level from one period to the next, usually measured over 12 months.
A fall in the general price level; prices are going down rather than up.
A slowdown in the rate of inflation — prices are still rising, but more slowly than before.
A measure of inflation that tracks the average change in prices paid by consumers for a representative basket of goods and services.
A situation where inflation is low, stable and predictable, allowing households, firms and government to plan with confidence.
